title: 2 Corinthians 6:11–18
context: Paul opens his heart to the Corinthians and asks them to open theirs in return. He warns them not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for righteousness and iniquity, light and darkness, Christ and Belial have nothing in common. The church is the temple of the living God, called to separate from idolatry and enjoy God as Father. Both traditions share this call to holiness; differences here are mainly about application.

verses.text: Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians. Our heart is enlarged.
verses.arminianNotes: Our mouth is open to you; our heart is enlarged. Arminian readers see Paul’s frank affection for a church that has doubted him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see pastoral warmth: Paul’s openness invites reconciliation between apostle and church.

verses.text: You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted by your own affections.
verses.arminianNotes: You are not restricted by us but by your own affections. Arminian readers see the problem lying in the Corinthians’ hearts, not Paul’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The barrier is their narrow affection.

verses.text: Now in return—I speak as to my children—you also open your hearts.
verses.arminianNotes: Open your hearts in return, as my children. Arminian readers see a fatherly plea for mutual love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same pastoral appeal.

verses.text: Don’t be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for what fellowship do righteousness and iniquity have? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?
verses.arminianNotes: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Arminian readers see a call to avoid binding partnerships that compromise devotion to Christ. Many apply it to marriage and other close alliances.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also apply it broadly, while noting that the immediate concern is idolatry (v.16). Righteousness and iniquity, light and darkness, cannot share the same allegiance.

verses.text: What agreement does Christ have with Belial? Or what portion does a believer have with an unbeliever?
verses.arminianNotes: What agreement has Christ with Belial? Arminian readers see stark spiritual opposition between Christ and evil powers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree; Belial is a name for Satan or worthlessness.

verses.text: What agreement does a temple of God have with idols? For you are a temple of the living God. Even as God said, “I will dwell in them and walk in them. I will be their God and they will be my people.”
verses.arminianNotes: You are a temple of the living God. Arminian readers see God dwelling among His people as the ground of their call to holiness. The WEB reads you are; many critical editions read we are, with the same point.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant promises from Leviticus 26:12 and Ezekiel 37:27 fulfilled in the church. The variant between you and we does not change the meaning: God’s people are His dwelling.

verses.text: Therefore “ ‘Come out from among them, and be separate,’ says the Lord. ‘Touch no unclean thing. I will receive you.
verses.arminianNotes: Come out and be separate. Arminian readers see a call to holiness and separation from idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same call drawn from Isaiah 52:11, applied to the church.

verses.text: I will be to you a Father. You will be to me sons and daughters,’ says the Lord Almighty.”
verses.arminianNotes: I will be a Father to you, and you will be my sons and daughters. Arminian readers rejoice in adoption into God’s family, open to all who come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see adoption as a covenant blessing secured by grace, echoing 2 Samuel 7:14.
